title: EverGreen Packaging: lean practices, cost of quality and sustainability reporting
participant_role: Management accountant at a packaging manufacturer evaluating JIT, TQM and a customer's sustainability reporting request
judge_role: Chief operating officer of EverGreen Packaging, an engineer who must present the proposals to the board of directors

difficulty.rationale: JIT savings, cost of quality and sustainability reporting.

scenario:
You are to assume the role of management accountant for EVERGREEN PACKAGING, a manufacturer of corrugated cardboard boxes for retailers and online sellers. The chief operating officer (judge) has asked you to review three proposals before the next leadership meeting.

EVERGREEN PACKAGING has grown quickly, and the chief operating officer (judge) believes the company is wasting money in the plant. The warehouse is full of raw materials and finished boxes, and a large share of each month's output must be scrapped or reworked. Some boxes that pass inspection are still returned by customers.

The operations team has proposed moving to just-in-time (JIT) purchasing and production. The quality team has proposed a total quality management (TQM) program. At the same time, the company's largest retail customer has asked every supplier to report sustainability data each year and has said it prefers suppliers who provide it.

[Just-in-time proposal: see exhibits]

[Cost of quality, last year: see exhibits]

[Customer sustainability request: see exhibits]

The chief operating officer (judge) is an engineer, not an accountant, and will present your findings to the board of directors next month. The chief operating officer (judge) wants to know whether the numbers support these changes, what could go wrong and how the accounting department's work would change.

You must:
- Explain how JIT, TQM and lean practices affect managerial accounting
- Evaluate the savings and risks of the JIT proposal
- Analyze the cost of quality and the TQM proposal
- Explain non-traditional uses of financial information, including sustainability reporting
- Discuss the role of ethics in reporting results and managing risk

You will present your analysis to the chief operating officer (judge) in a role-play to take place in the chief operating officer's (judge's) office. The chief operating officer (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented your analysis and have answered the chief operating officer's (judge's) questions, the chief operating officer (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

solution.overview: A strong answer explains that managerial accounting serves internal decision makers and must change when the plant goes lean. JIT saves $240,000 of carrying cost, or $190,000 net of the supplier charge, but adds stockout risk. The cost of quality is $600,000, of which $470,000 (about 78%) is failure cost, and TQM saves a net $85,000 a year. The presenter explains sustainability reporting as a non-traditional use of accounting data, stresses honest reporting to avoid greenwashing, and speaks in plain, board-ready language for an engineer audience.

by_task.task: How JIT, TQM and lean affect managerial accounting
answer: Managerial accounting gives internal managers information to plan, control and make decisions; it is not bound by GAAP and looks forward
JIT and lean shrink inventory, so there are fewer inventory accounts, fewer transactions to track and smaller variances to explain
Costing can shift to value stream costing, which assigns costs to a whole product flow instead of each job or department
Performance measures move beyond cost variances to cycle time, on-time delivery, defect rates and inventory turnover
TQM adds a cost of quality report so managers can see what poor quality really costs
Carrying cost today: $2,000,000 x 20% = $400,000
JIT cuts average inventory 60% to $800,000, so carrying cost falls to $160,000, a saving of $240,000
Net of the $50,000 supplier charge, JIT saves $190,000 a year and frees $1,200,000 of cash tied up in inventory
Risks: stockouts, supplier delays or disruptions, and lost sales if a big order cannot be filled
Reduce risk with reliable, nearby suppliers, clear contracts and a small safety stock for key materials
Failure costs are $470,000, about 78% of the total, so EverGreen spends mostly on fixing mistakes instead of preventing them
TQM cuts failure costs 50%, or $235,000, while adding $150,000 of prevention, for a net saving of $85,000 a year
External failures also cost customer goodwill, which is not in these numbers, so the true benefit is likely larger
Accounting systems can measure non-financial data such as energy use, recycled content and emissions per 1,000 boxes
Sustainability reporting helps keep the large retail customer and can attract investors and lenders
Lean metrics and value stream reports help managers see waste; activity-based costing shows which products or customers really use the most resources
Use the same careful controls for this data as for financial data: clear definitions, consistent methods and documentation
Ethical reporting builds trust; overstating green results (greenwashing) can cost customers and bring legal or regulatory trouble
Report only what can be measured and supported, use the same method every year and disclose estimates
Consider outside assurance of the sustainability data as it becomes important to customers
Be honest about JIT and TQM risks with the board instead of showing only the best case
For the board, lead with the bottom line ($190,000 and $85,000 a year), use one simple chart and avoid accounting jargon

judge_question_answers.question: If we cut inspection costs, won't quality get worse?
answer: Not if the money moves to prevention: TQM builds quality into the process instead of inspecting defects out at the end
Our failure costs are $470,000, almost six times appraisal, so inspection alone is not working
Reduce inspection gradually and only where defect rates prove the process is under control
Track defect rates, returns and scrap monthly so we can react quickly if quality slips

judge_question_answers.question: Our competitor claims to be carbon neutral. Should we just say the same?
answer: No: we should only make claims we can measure and support
An unsupported claim is greenwashing and could mislead customers, damage trust and bring legal or regulatory action
Start by measuring our real energy use and emissions per 1,000 boxes and report them honestly
Set realistic reduction goals and consider outside assurance before making public claims

key_concepts.definition: Accounting that provides information to internal managers for planning, controlling and decision making. It is future focused and does not have to follow GAAP.
A system that buys materials and makes products only as they are needed, which keeps inventory and carrying costs low.
The yearly cost of holding inventory, such as storage, insurance, handling and the cost of money tied up. Often stated as a percentage of average inventory.
An approach that removes waste (extra inventory, waiting, defects, extra steps) from every process.
A company-wide effort to improve quality continuously so that defects are prevented rather than found later.
The total of prevention, appraisal, internal failure and external failure costs.
Prevention costs stop defects before they happen (training, maintenance). Appraisal costs find defects through inspection and testing.
Internal failure costs come from defects found before shipping (scrap, rework). External failure costs come from defects found by customers (returns, replacements, lost sales).
A lean costing method that assigns costs to an entire product flow instead of individual jobs or departments.
Reporting environmental and social data, such as energy use and emissions, alongside financial results.
Making environmental claims that are false, exaggerated or unsupported.

notes: ICDC level because students must connect operations concepts to managerial accounting, run two separate cost analyses and address ethics and audience in one presentation. Watch for students who forget to subtract the $50,000 supplier charge or the $150,000 of new prevention spending, or who call the whole $600,000 cost of quality wasteful.

items.label: Explain the impact of business operational practices on managerial accounting

criteria.exceeds: Shows that JIT saves $240,000 of carrying cost ($190,000 net of the $50,000 supplier charge) and frees $1,200,000 of cash, and that TQM cuts failure costs by $235,000 for a net $85,000 saving, then explains how lean changes the accounting work (fewer inventory accounts, value stream costing, measures like cycle time and defect rates) and how to manage stockout risk.
criteria.meets: Calculates the $190,000 net JIT saving and the $85,000 net TQM saving, names stockout and supplier delay risks, and explains that lean means fewer inventory transactions and a cost of quality report.
criteria.below: Gets part of the analysis, for example reports the $240,000 JIT saving without subtracting the $50,000 supplier charge or the $235,000 TQM saving without subtracting the $150,000 of new prevention spending.
criteria.little: Does not calculate the JIT or TQM savings, or does not connect JIT, TQM and lean to accounting at all.

items.label: Discuss non-traditional uses for financial information

criteria.exceeds: Explains that the accounting system can track recycled content, energy use and carbon emissions per 1,000 boxes for the largest customer, that this data can help keep that customer and attract investors and lenders, and that it needs the same controls as financial data (clear definitions, consistent methods, documentation), plus other uses such as lean metrics and activity-based costing.
criteria.meets: Describes sustainability reporting as a non-traditional use of accounting data, names the data the customer requested and explains that reporting it helps keep the customer.
criteria.below: Mentions sustainability reporting in general terms without the requested data, the business benefit or the need for controls.
criteria.little: Does not address non-traditional uses of financial information or ignores the customer's request.

items.label: Explain the role of ethics in risk management

criteria.exceeds: Explains that overstating green results is greenwashing that can cost customers and bring legal or regulatory trouble, recommends reporting only measured and supported data with the same method each year and outside assurance, and urges an honest view of JIT and TQM risks for the board instead of only the best case.
criteria.meets: Explains that ethical, honest reporting builds trust and reduces risk, warns against greenwashing and says the board should hear the risks of JIT and TQM as well as the savings.
criteria.below: Says ethics matters in general terms without linking it to the sustainability data or to the risks in the proposals.
criteria.little: Does not discuss ethics, or suggests making claims or showing results that cannot be supported.

items.label: Explain the nature of managerial accounting

criteria.exceeds: Explains that managerial accounting gives internal managers forward-looking information to plan, control and decide, is not bound by GAAP, and must change when the plant goes lean, using the $600,000 cost of quality report (with $470,000, about 78%, in failure costs) as an example of information that guides decisions.
criteria.meets: States that managerial accounting serves internal decision makers, is not bound by GAAP, and presents the $600,000 total cost of quality with $470,000 of failure costs.
criteria.below: Confuses managerial accounting with financial reporting, or gets the cost of quality total or failure share wrong or calls the whole $600,000 wasteful.
criteria.little: Does not explain what managerial accounting is or how it supports these decisions.

items.label: Employ communication styles appropriate to target audience

criteria.exceeds: Speaks to the COO as an engineer preparing for the board: leads with the bottom line ($190,000 and $85,000 a year), uses one simple chart or comparison, avoids accounting jargon and frames the points so the COO can repeat them to the board.
criteria.meets: Uses plain language, defines terms like carrying cost and cost of quality, and gives the COO clear bottom-line numbers.
criteria.below: Relies on accounting jargon or detailed steps without explaining them, so the key results are hard for a non-accountant to find.
criteria.little: Communication does not suit the audience and the COO could not present the findings to the board.

items.label: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking

criteria.exceeds: Connects the three proposals, for example that JIT only works if TQM reduces defects, and that external failures also cost customer goodwill not shown in the numbers.
criteria.meets: Reasons correctly from the exhibits to the JIT and TQM savings and the risks of each.
criteria.below: Reaches conclusions without showing the reasoning, or treats the proposals as unrelated.

items.label: Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems

criteria.exceeds: Recommends moving ahead with JIT and TQM with safeguards (reliable nearby suppliers, clear contracts, a small safety stock) and starting honest sustainability reporting for the customer.
criteria.meets: Makes clear recommendations on JIT, TQM and the sustainability request supported by the numbers.
criteria.below: Gives recommendations that are vague, partly supported or missing for one of the proposals.

criteria.exceeds: Covers all three proposals in a logical order with confident, professional delivery and board-ready wording.
criteria.meets: Presents the savings, risks, sustainability reporting and ethics clearly and in an organized way.
criteria.below: Presentation is hard to follow, skips a proposal or runs out of time.

items.label: Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity

criteria.exceeds: Uses an effective visual, such as a chart of the four cost of quality categories before and after TQM ($600,000 to $515,000), and adds useful ideas such as value stream costing or new lean performance measures.
criteria.meets: Organizes the numbers in a way that makes the savings easy to understand.
criteria.below: Presents the facts with little effort to make them engaging or easy to follow.
criteria.little: Shows no evidence of creativity or original thought.

items.label: Overall impression and responses to the judge's questions

criteria.exceeds: Answers both questions correctly and confidently: moving money to prevention builds quality in, failure costs of $470,000 are almost six times appraisal, and inspection should drop gradually while defects are tracked monthly; and the company should not claim carbon neutrality without support, but measure real emissions per 1,000 boxes, report honestly, set goals and consider outside assurance.
criteria.meets: Answers both questions mostly correctly, including that prevention replaces inspection and that an unsupported carbon neutral claim would be greenwashing.
criteria.below: Answers only one question correctly, or gives vague answers without the numbers or the risks.
criteria.little: Cannot answer the judge's questions, or agrees to copy the competitor's carbon neutral claim.

key_points: Managerial accounting serves internal decision makers, looks forward and is not bound by GAAP; lean changes what it tracks (value stream costing, cycle time, defect rates)
JIT: carrying cost falls from $400,000 to $160,000, a $240,000 saving, or $190,000 net of the $50,000 supplier charge, and frees $1,200,000 of cash
JIT risks: stockouts, supplier delays and lost sales; reduce them with reliable suppliers, clear contracts and a small safety stock
Cost of quality is $600,000, of which $470,000 (about 78%) is internal and external failure cost
TQM cuts failure costs by $235,000 while adding $150,000 of prevention, a net saving of $85,000 a year (new cost of quality $515,000)
Sustainability reporting (recycled content, energy use, emissions per 1,000 boxes) is a non-traditional use of accounting data that needs the same controls as financial data
Report only what can be measured and supported; unsupported green claims are greenwashing and create legal and customer risk
For the board, lead with the bottom line ($190,000 and $85,000 a year) in plain language
